blocks.content: 1. Why Estimation Matters

Every meaningful design decision, one server or a hundred, a single database or a sharded cluster, a cache or no cache at all, depends entirely on scale. A system serving a thousand users and a system serving a billion users can look completely different in their architecture even if they solve the exact same problem on paper.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272892129-714500167.png
blocks.alt: The right architecture for a problem is inseparable from the scale it actually needs to run at

blocks.content: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is the practice of quickly approximating that scale, traffic, storage, bandwidth, and memory, using rough, defensible numbers, before committing to any specific design. It is not about precision, it is about getting close enough, fast enough, to make the next design decision with real numbers behind it instead of a guess.

blocks.title: Why Interviewers Ask For This
blocks.content: In a system design interview, estimation is not a formality before the "real" design work starts, it is the evidence that every subsequent design choice, sharding, caching, replication, is actually justified by the scale of the problem rather than picked at random.
2. The Four Things You Estimate
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272894249-33390315.png
blocks.alt: Nearly every estimation exercise reduces to these same four numbers

blocks.content: ["Traffic: how many requests per second the system must handle, both on average and at peak","Storage: how much data accumulates over a given retention period","Bandwidth: how much data moves in and out of the system per second","Memory: how much of the hottest data needs to live in cache or RAM rather than be fetched from disk on every request"]
items: Traffic: how many requests per second the system must handle, both on average and at peak
Storage: how much data accumulates over a given retention period
Bandwidth: how much data moves in and out of the system per second
Memory: how much of the hottest data needs to live in cache or RAM rather than be fetched from disk on every request

blocks.content: 3. Numbers Worth Memorizing
A handful of reference numbers make every estimate faster, because you stop re-deriving basic conversions mid-interview and spend that time on the actual design instead.

{"headers":["Time Unit","Approximate Seconds"],"rows":[["1 day","86,400 seconds (round to 100,000 for quick mental math)"],["1 month","about 2.6 million seconds"],["1 year","about 31.5 million seconds"]]}

{"headers":["Typical Object","Approximate Size"],"rows":[["A short text message or tweet","~300 bytes"],["A JSON API response","~1 to 5 KB"],["A compressed thumbnail image","~50 to 200 KB"],["A full-resolution photo","~2 to 5 MB"],["A minute of standard-definition video","~5 to 10 MB"]]}
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272895953-104840713.png
blocks.alt: Rounding 86,400 seconds per day to a clean 100,000 costs only about 13 percent of accuracy and saves real time under pressure

blocks.title: Round Aggressively
blocks.content: Dividing by 100,000 instead of 86,400 makes every traffic calculation a one-step mental shortcut, and the resulting 13 percent overestimate is well within the margin of error every other assumption in the exercise already carries.
4. Latency Numbers Every Engineer Should Know
blocks.text: 4. Latency Numbers Every Engineer Should Know

blocks.content: Knowing the relative cost of different operations is what lets an estimate turn into an actual design decision, for example recognizing that a cross-region network call is roughly 100,000 times slower than an L1 cache reference is what justifies adding a cache in the first place.

{"headers":["Operation","Approximate Latency"],"rows":[["L1 cache reference","~1 nanosecond"],["Main memory (RAM) reference","~100 nanoseconds"],["SSD random read","~100 microseconds"],["Round trip within the same data center","~500 microseconds"],["Disk seek (spinning HDD)","~10 milliseconds"],["Round trip between two continents","~150 milliseconds"]]}

The gaps between these rows are not small, they are multiple orders of magnitude each, which is exactly why caching frequently-read data in memory, or serving users from a region close to them, produces such dramatic real-world improvements.
5. The Four-Step Estimation Framework
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026162-639211788.png
blocks.alt: The same four-step sequence works for nearly any system design estimation problem

blocks.content: Step 1: Clarify and State Assumptions Out Loud
blocks.text: Step 1: Clarify and State Assumptions Out Loud

blocks.content: Before any math, state the assumptions the rest of the estimate depends on: total users, daily active users, how often an average user performs the relevant action, and how long data must be retained. Getting these numbers exactly right matters far less than stating them clearly, so the interviewer or teammate can follow and challenge the reasoning.
Step 2: Traffic Estimation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026911-695354114.png
blocks.alt: Daily active users times actions per day, divided into a per-second rate, then scaled up for peak load

blocks.content: Example

100 million daily active users, each performing 10 read actions per day: 100,000,000 x 10 = 1,000,000,000 reads per day. Dividing by roughly 100,000 seconds per day gives about 10,000 average reads per second. Real traffic is never flat across the day, so multiply by a peak factor, commonly 2 to 3x, giving a peak of roughly 20,000 to 30,000 reads per second.
Step 3: Storage Estimation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027097-232367340.png
blocks.alt: New records per day times average record size, then multiplied out across however long the data must be retained

blocks.content: Example
1 million new records per day, each 1 KB: 1,000,000 x 1 KB = 1 GB of new data per day. Over 5 years: 1 GB x 365 x 5 = ~1.8 TB total, before accounting for replication or index overhead.
Easy Interview Trick

State the daily figure first, then multiply by the retention period last, this makes it trivial to recompute the total on the spot if the interviewer changes the retention assumption, without redoing the whole calculation from scratch.
Step 4: Bandwidth Estimation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272902650-377021763.png
blocks.alt: Peak requests per second times the average size of each request or response

blocks.content: Example

30,000 peak reads per second, each returning a 2 KB response: 30,000 x 2 KB = 60 MB/s, or about 480 Mbps, a number that immediately tells you whether a single server's network interface can handle it or whether the traffic must be spread across multiple servers.
Easy Interview Trick
Bandwidth estimates reuse the peak traffic number already computed in Step 2, there is no need to separately estimate traffic for this step, only the payload size is new.

The example below implements exactly this four-step framework as a small, reusable calculator: given daily active users, actions per user, average payload size, a peak factor, and a retention period, it computes average QPS, peak QPS, daily storage, total storage, and peak bandwidth, the same five numbers every estimation exercise in this topic produces by hand.

codes.python:
class EstimationResult:
    def __init__(self):
        self.avg_qps = 0.0
        self.peak_qps = 0.0
        self.daily_storage_gb = 0.0
        self.total_storage_gb = 0.0
        self.peak_bandwidth_mbps = 0.0


def estimate(daily_active_users, actions_per_user_per_day, avg_payload_bytes, peak_factor, retention_years):
    result = EstimationResult()

    total_actions_per_day = daily_active_users * actions_per_user_per_day
    result.avg_qps = total_actions_per_day / 86400.0
    result.peak_qps = result.avg_qps * peak_factor

    daily_bytes = total_actions_per_day * avg_payload_bytes
    result.daily_storage_gb = daily_bytes / 1_000_000_000.0
    result.total_storage_gb = result.daily_storage_gb * 365 * retention_years

    peak_bytes_per_second = result.peak_qps * avg_payload_bytes
    result.peak_bandwidth_mbps = peak_bytes_per_second / 1_000_000.0

    return result


def main():
    # 100M DAU, 10 reads/user/day, 2KB per response, 3x peak factor, 5 year retention.
    r = estimate(100_000_000, 10, 2048, 3.0, 5)

    print(f"Average QPS: {r.avg_qps:.0f}")
    print(f"Peak QPS: {r.peak_qps:.0f}")
    print(f"Daily storage: {r.daily_storage_gb:.2f} GB")
    print(f"Total storage over retention: {r.total_storage_gb:.0f} GB")
    print(f"Peak bandwidth: {r.peak_bandwidth_mbps:.2f} MB/s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

blocks.content: 6. Worked Example 1: A Twitter-Like Feed
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272904380-141460622.png
blocks.alt: 300 million daily active users produces very different traffic, storage, and bandwidth profiles

blocks.content: Assumptions: 300 million DAU, each user reads their feed 5 times per day and posts 1 tweet per day, each tweet stored as roughly 300 bytes, retained for 5 years.
Traffic

Reads: 300,000,000 x 5 = 1.5 billion reads/day, or about 15,000 average reads/second (using the rounded 100,000-second day), peaking around 30,000 to 45,000/second at a 2 to 3x peak factor. Writes: 300,000,000 x 1 = 300 million writes/day, about 3,000 average writes/second, dwarfed by read traffic.
Storage
300 million tweets/day x 300 bytes = 90 GB of new tweet data per day. Over 5 years: 90 GB x 365 x 5 = ~164 TB, before replication factor or indexes, which commonly add another 2 to 3x on top.
Bandwidth

At peak 30,000 reads/second, each returning a feed payload of roughly 5 KB (several tweets bundled per request): 30,000 x 5 KB = 150 MB/s, about 1.2 Gbps, clearly justifying multiple servers behind a load balancer rather than one.
7. Worked Example 2: A URL Shortener
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272905997-584792950.png
blocks.alt: A much smaller, read-heavy system produces a very different profile from the feed example above

blocks.content: Assumptions: 100 million DAU, 1 million new short URLs created per day, each short URL redirected roughly 100 times per day on average, each URL record about 500 bytes, stored indefinitely.
Traffic

Writes: 1,000,000 new URLs/day, about 10 writes/second average, trivially low. Reads (redirects): 1,000,000 x 100 = 100 million redirects/day, about 1,000 average reads/second, peaking around 2,000 to 3,000/second, a read-to-write ratio of roughly 100 to 1.
Storage

1,000,000 x 500 bytes = 500 MB of new records per day. Stored indefinitely rather than for a fixed retention window, so after 5 years: 500 MB x 365 x 5 = ~900 GB, small enough that a single well-indexed database can plausibly hold the entire dataset.
Bandwidth

A redirect response carries essentially no body, just an HTTP 301 with a Location header, so bandwidth stays low even at thousands of requests per second, this system is bottlenecked by request count and lookup latency, not payload size.
8. Reading Your Own Numbers: What They Actually Tell You
blocks.text: 8. Reading Your Own Numbers: What They Actually Tell You

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272907976-604882380.png
blocks.alt: Whether reads or writes dominate is itself one of the most important design decisions your estimate reveals

blocks.content: The two worked examples above land on opposite ends of the same question: the feed system and the URL shortener are both read-heavy, but for different reasons and at different scales, while a system like a logging or analytics pipeline would flip the ratio entirely and be write-heavy instead.

{"headers":["Pattern","What The Numbers Suggest","Example"],"rows":[["Heavily read-dominant","Invest in caching and read replicas before anything else","Social feeds, URL redirects, product catalogs"],["Heavily write-dominant","Invest in write throughput, batching, and sharding before read optimization","Logging pipelines, IoT sensor ingestion, analytics events"],["Roughly balanced","Both paths need attention, often the hardest case to design for cheaply","Collaborative editing, chat systems, multiplayer games"]]}
9. Common Estimation Patterns Worth Recognizing

{"headers":["Pattern","Quick Rule"],"rows":[["Requests/day to requests/second","Divide by 100,000 (rounded from 86,400)"],["Records x size to storage","Multiply straight through, then scale by retention period last"],["Peak vs average traffic","Peak factor of 2 to 3x average is a safe, commonly used default"],["Storage overhead from replication","Multiply raw storage by the replication factor, commonly 3x"]]}

blocks.title: Server Capacity Rules of Thumb
blocks.content: A modest 8-core, 16 GB web server can typically handle roughly 10,000 simple API requests per second, or closer to 1,000 per second if each request is database-heavy. A typical database server manages roughly 1,000 writes per second and 10,000 indexed reads per second, numbers precise enough to sanity-check whether an estimate implies 2 servers or 200.
10. Tips for System Design Interviews
1. State Assumptions Out Loud

Never silently assume a number, say it explicitly: "I'll assume 50 million daily active users", so the interviewer can correct it immediately if the real number should be different, rather than watching an entire estimate go sideways from one unstated guess.
2. Round Aggressively
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272909933-225087430.png
blocks.alt: Extra decimal places rarely change which architecture is the right one

blocks.content: 100,000 instead of 86,400, 1,000 instead of 1,024, these roundings introduce single-digit percentage error and buy back real time for the parts of the interview that actually differentiate a strong answer.
3. Show the Math Step by Step
blocks.text: 3. Show the Math Step by Step

blocks.content: Write out each multiplication rather than jumping straight to a final number, an interviewer following along can catch a mistake early, and a wrong final number with visible correct reasoning throughout is judged far more favorably than an unexplained right answer.
4. Connect Numbers to Design Decisions

An estimate that is never used is wasted effort, explicitly say what a number implies: "At 30,000 peak QPS, a single server handling 10,000 requests/second means we need at least 3 behind a load balancer."
5. Avoid Paralysis by Precision
Spending five minutes nailing down whether peak QPS is 28,000 or 31,000 is time that rarely changes which architecture gets chosen, and is time not spent on the actual system design that follows.
6. Avoid Skipping to the Answer
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396027285-526381027.png
blocks.alt: A design choice with no number behind it looks the same to an interviewer whether it was reasoned or guessed

blocks.content: Announcing "we'll need sharding" without first showing the traffic or storage number that actually requires it leaves the interviewer unable to tell whether that conclusion was reasoned through or simply memorized from a previous interview.
Common Mistakes

["Treating estimation as a box-checking formality instead of using the resulting numbers to justify every later design decision","Computing an over-precise final number (28,417 QPS) that took real time to produce but changes nothing about the resulting architecture","Forgetting the peak factor entirely and sizing a system only for its average load, which then falls over during the very traffic spikes it needs to survive","Estimating storage without ever multiplying by the retention period, silently underestimating total footprint by an order of magnitude or more","Skipping straight to naming technologies (\"we'll use Kafka and Cassandra\") before any number has actually shown those tools are necessary at this scale"]
items: Treating estimation as a box-checking formality instead of using the resulting numbers to justify every later design decision
Computing an over-precise final number (28,417 QPS) that took real time to produce but changes nothing about the resulting architecture
Forgetting the peak factor entirely and sizing a system only for its average load, which then falls over during the very traffic spikes it needs to survive
Estimating storage without ever multiplying by the retention period, silently underestimating total footprint by an order of magnitude or more
Skipping straight to naming technologies ("we'll use Kafka and Cassandra") before any number has actually shown those tools are necessary at this scale

blocks.content: Practice

Estimate traffic, storage, and bandwidth for a video streaming platform with 50 million DAU, where each user watches an average of 3 videos per day, each video is roughly 100 MB, and viewing history is retained for 2 years.

Then, using the same four-step framework, estimate the numbers for a ride-sharing app with 20 million DAU, where each user requests an average of 0.5 rides per day, each ride record is 2 KB, and ride history must be retained for 7 years for compliance reasons.
For each of the two systems above, state explicitly whether it is read-heavy or write-heavy, and what that specifically implies about where to invest engineering effort first.
Key Takeaways

Back-of-the-envelope estimation turns an ambiguous system design problem into concrete numbers, traffic, storage, and bandwidth, using a repeatable four-step framework: clarify assumptions, estimate traffic, estimate storage, estimate bandwidth. Precision is never the goal, one significant figure is almost always enough, and every number should exist to justify a specific design decision rather than to demonstrate arithmetic.

The two worked examples in this topic, a feed system and a URL shortener, show how differently the same framework plays out depending on whether reads or writes dominate, exactly the kind of concrete grounding that turns the qualitative tradeoffs from the CAP Theorem and Consistency Models topics into an actual, sized architecture rather than an abstract discussion.
